Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verses 5–9:

﴿Shall We then turn away from you the Reminder (al-dhikr) altogether, because you are a people who exceed the limits?﴾ It is said: "I struck away from him" (ḍaraba ʿanhu) and "I turned away from him" (aḍraba ʿanhu) when one leaves him and refrains from him. And "ṣafḥ" (turning away) is the verbal noun of their saying "ṣafaḥtu ʿanhu," when you turn away from him, which is by turning to him the side of your face [and his neck]. [[Omitted from manuscript "A".]] The "Reminder" here means the Qur'an. Its meaning: Shall We withhold the revelation from you, refrain from sending down the Qur'an, and so not command you [nor forbid you] [[Omitted from manuscript "A".]] because you have gone to excess in your disbelief and abandoned faith? It is an interrogative with the sense of denial, meaning: We will not do that. This is the view of Qatadah and a group of scholars.

Qatadah said: "By Allah, if this Qur'an had been lifted when the first of this nation rejected it, they would have perished. But Allah returned to them with His kindness and mercy, and repeated it to them for twenty years, or as long as Allah willed."  [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 25/49.]]

It has also been said: its meaning is, "Shall We turn away from you, by not reminding you, turning aside in aversion?"

Al-Kisa'i said: "Shall We fold up the Reminder from you, folding it up, so that you are neither called nor admonished?" Al-Kalbi said: "Shall We leave you neglected, not commanding you nor forbidding you?" Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "Shall We turn away from you and leave you, so that We do not punish you for your disbelief?" [[See: al-Tabari: 25/49.]]

﴿Because you are a people who exceed the limits.﴾ The people of Madinah, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "in kuntum" (إِنْ كُنْتُمْ) with a kasrah on the hamzah, in the sense of "idh kuntum" (since you were), like His saying: "And you shall be the uppermost if you are believers" [Al 'Imran: 139]. The others read it with a fathah, in the sense of "li-anna kuntum qawman musrifin" (because you are a people who exceed the limits) [mushrikin (polytheists)] [[Addition from manuscript "B".]].

﴿How many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples?﴾ And there never came to them, ﴿any prophet but they mocked him,﴾ like the mockery of your people toward you, consoling His Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿So We destroyed those who were mightier in strength than them﴾ meaning stronger than your people, referring to the earlier ones who were destroyed for denying the messengers, ﴿and the example of the earlier peoples has passed on.﴾ That is, their attribute, their way, and their punishment; so the end of these people is likewise in destruction.

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "The Mighty, the All-Knowing created them."﴾ That is, if you asked your people, they acknowledged that Allah is their Creator, and acknowledged His might and knowledge, yet they worshipped other than Him and denied His power over resurrection, due to their extreme ignorance. Here the report about them is complete.

Then he began, pointing to Himself through His own creation, and said: ﴿He who made the earth a cradle for you and made for you in it roads, that you may be guided﴾, to your destinations in your journeys.

﴿And He who sent down water from the sky in measure﴾, that is, in the measure of your need for it, not as He sent it down upon the people of Noah without measure, until He destroyed them.

﴿So We revived with it a dead land. Thus﴾, that is, just as We revived this dead land with rain, ﴿you will be brought forth﴾ from your graves alive.

﴿And He who created all the pairs﴾, that is, all the kinds, ﴿and made for you ships and cattle on which you ride﴾, on land and sea.

﴿That you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾. The pronoun is in the masculine form (ʿalayhi) because it refers back to "mā" (that which), which is grammatically masculine in this usage.

﴿Then you remember the favour of your Lord when you are settled upon them﴾, by His subjecting the vehicles on land and sea to you, ﴿and say: "Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, and we could not have controlled it [by ourselves]"﴾. "Subjected" means made it tame for us. "Could not have controlled it" means were not able to master it. It was also said: were not capable of restraining it.

﴿And indeed, to our Lord we will surely return﴾, that is, we will certainly be turned back toward Him in the Return.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verses 15–18:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿And they have attributed to Him a portion (juz') of His servants﴾. That is, a share and a part. This is their saying: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." The meaning of *al-ja'l* (making, ascribing) here is to pass a judgment about a thing and to declare it, as you say: "I made Zayd the best of people," meaning: I described him and I judged him to be so. ﴿Indeed, man﴾ means the disbeliever, ﴿is clearly ungrateful﴾ (kafur), denying the favours of Allah, ﴿manifestly﴾ (mubin), clearly showing ingratitude.

﴿Has He taken daughters from what He creates and chosen sons for you?﴾ This is a rhetorical question of rebuke and denial. It says: "Has your Lord taken daughters for Himself, and chosen sons for you?" Like His saying: "Has your Lord chosen sons for you?" [al-Isra': 40].

﴿And when one of them is given good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness﴾, that is, of that which they have made a likeness for Allah. This is because the offspring of everything resembles it. That is, when one of them is given the good news of daughters, as mentioned in Surat al-Nahl: ﴿And when one of them is given the good news of a female, his face becomes dark and he suppresses grief﴾ [al-Nahl: 58], from sorrow and rage.

﴿Or is one who is brought up among ornaments﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs recited *yunasha'* with a *ḍamma* on the *yā'*, a *fatḥa* on the *nūn* and a *shaddah* on the *shīn*, meaning "is raised" (yurabba). The others recited it with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'*, a *sukūn* on the *nūn* and no *shaddah* on the *shīn*, meaning "grows up and matures" (yanbutu wa yakbaru). ﴿Among ornaments﴾ means in adornment, referring to women. ﴿And he is not clear in dispute﴾ means he is not clear in argument because of their weakness and foolishness. Qatadah said regarding this verse: "A woman rarely speaks wanting to present her proof, except that she speaks in a way that is a proof against her."[[Reported by al-Tabari (25/57), and ʿAbd al-Razzaq in his Tafsir (2/195). al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (7/370) attributed it also to ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir.]]

There are three possible grammatical positions for *man* (مَنْ). The first is the nominative (*al-raf'*) by way of inception (*al-ibtida'*, the subject of a nominal sentence). The second is the accusative (*al-nasb*) by way of an implied verb (*al-idmar*); its sense is: "or [do they ascribe to Him] one who is raised among ornaments, they make him a daughter of Allah." The third is the genitive (*al-khafd*), by way of coordination with the earlier words: ﴿from what He creates﴾ and ﴿that which he attributes﴾.

There are three possible grammatical positions for *man* (مَنْ). The first is the nominative (*al-raf'*) by way of inception (*al-ibtida'*, the subject of a nominal sentence). The second is the accusative (*al-nasb*) by way of an implied verb (*al-idmar*); its sense is: "or [do they ascribe to Him] one who is raised among ornaments, they make him a daughter of Allah." The third is the genitive (*al-khafd*), by way of coordination with the earlier words: ﴿from what He creates﴾ and ﴿that which he attributes﴾.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verses 22–28:

﴿Nay, they say: "We found our fathers following a community (ummah)"﴾ — upon a religion and a creed (millah). Mujahid said: "upon an imam (leader)." ﴿And we are indeed following in their footsteps, guided﴾ — they made themselves guided by following their fathers.

﴿And thus We did not send before you any warner into a town but its affluent ones (mutrafun) said: "We found our fathers upon a community, and we are indeed following in their footsteps"﴾ — its affluent ones (aghniya') and its leaders (ru'asa'). ﴿...following in their footsteps﴾ — following them.

﴿Say (qul)﴾ — Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read "qala" (he said) as a report, while the others read "qul" (say) as a command. ﴿Even if I brought you something better guiding than what you found your fathers upon?﴾ — Abu Ja'far read "ji'naakum" (We brought you) in the plural, while the others read "ji'tukum" (I brought you) in the singular. ﴿Better guiding﴾ — a more correct religion. ﴿Than what you found your fathers upon﴾ — al-Zajjaj said: Say to them, [O Muhammad]: [[Addition from "b".]] "Will you follow what you found your fathers upon, even if I bring you something better than it?" But they refused to accept, and ﴿they said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent."﴾

﴿So We took vengeance upon them; then observe how was the end of those who denied.﴾

The statement of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people: "Indeed, I am free (bara')"﴾ — meaning "bari'" (free/innocent). "Bara'" is neither dualized, pluralized, nor feminized, because it is a verbal noun (masdar) placed in the position of an adjective (na't).

﴿of what you worship﴾.

﴿Except He who created me﴾ — created me, ﴿for indeed He will guide me﴾ — He will guide me to His religion.

﴿And He made it﴾ — meaning this statement, ﴿a word remaining among his descendants﴾ — Mujahid and Qatadah said: it means the word of monotheism, which is "There is no god but Allah," a word remaining among his descendants, in his offspring. Qatadah said: there will always remain among his descendants those who worship Allah and affirm His oneness. Al-Qurazi said: it means that the bequest of Abraham, with which he enjoined his sons, remained in his progeny and descendants, and this is the statement of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132].

Ibn Zayd said: it means His statement: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131], and he recited: ﴿He named you "the Muslims"﴾ [al-Hajj: 78].

﴿That they may return﴾ — perhaps the people of Makkah will follow this religion and turn back from what they are upon to the religion of Abraham. Al-Suddi said: perhaps they will repent and return to the obedience of Allah, the Exalted and Majestic.

﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world,﴾ so We made this one wealthy and that one poor, this one a king and that one a slave. Just as We have given some of them preference over others in provision as We willed, so also We choose whom We will for the message.

﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees,﴾ through wealth and property, ﴿so that some of them may take others in service.﴾ That is, so that some of them may employ others. The wealthy, by their wealth, employ the poor laborers by their work, so that each becomes a means of livelihood for the other: this one with his wealth, and that one with his labor, and thus the affairs of the world are kept in order. Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: some of them own others through wealth, by way of slavery and ownership.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verses 36–37:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾ means: turns away (yu'ridu) from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, so he does not fear His punishment and does not hope for His reward. It is said: "I 'ashawtu ilá al-nar, a'shu 'ashwan" (I went towards the fire, guided by it) when I headed toward it seeking guidance by it, and "'ashawtu 'anhá" (I turned away from it), just as one says "'adaltu ilá fulān" and "'adaltu 'anhu," and "miltu ilayhi" and "miltu 'anhu." Al-Qurazi (al-Qurazi) said: he turns his back on the remembrance of the Most Merciful, which is the Qur'an. Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: he makes his sight dim by turning his gaze away from it. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad said: the origin of 'ashw is looking with weak sight. Ibn 'Abbas recited "wa man ya'sha" with a fatha on the shin, meaning ya'má (he becomes blind); it is said "'asha ya'shá 'ashan" when he became blind, so he is a'shá (blind), and a woman is 'ashwá'.

﴿We shall appoint for him a devil﴾: Ya'qub recited "yuqayyid" with the ya', and the rest with the nun, meaning: We shall assign to him a devil, join him to him, and give him power over him.

﴿So he is his companion﴾: he does not part from him; he makes blindness seem attractive to him and makes him imagine that he is upon guidance.

﴿And indeed they﴾ meaning the devils, ﴿surely bar them from the way﴾: i.e., they prevent them from guidance. He used the plural pronoun because His saying "And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We shall appoint for him a devil" is, in meaning, plural, even though the wording is singular. ﴿And they think that they are guided﴾: and the disbelievers among the children of Adam think that they are upon guidance.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verses 38–41:

﴿Until, when he comes to Us﴾ The people of Iraq (except Abu Bakr) read "jā'anā" (in the singular), meaning the disbelieving one. The others read "jā'ānā" (in the dual), meaning the disbeliever and his companion (qarīn), who are placed in one chain.

﴿He will say﴾ The disbeliever to his companion, the Shaytan: ﴿"Oh, would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts!"﴾ That is, the distance between the east and the west. The name of one of them was given precedence over the other, as one says "al-qamarān" for the sun and the moon, and "al-'Umarān" for Abu Bakr and 'Umar. It has also been said that he meant by "the two easts" the east of summer and the east of winter, but the first view is more sound. ﴿"Wretched is the companion!"﴾ Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: When the disbeliever is resurrected, he is paired with his companion from among the devils, and he does not part from him until they both arrive at the Fire. [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 25/74, and 'Abd al-Razzaq in his Tafsir: 2/196, both from Sa'id al-Juraysi, contrary to what is in the two manuscripts, which attribute the saying to Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. And al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur: 7/378 added its attribution to Ibn al-Mundhir.]]

﴿And it will not benefit you today﴾ in the Hereafter, ﴿since you wronged﴾ that is, you associated partners (with Allah) in the world, ﴿that you, in the punishment, will be sharing﴾. That is: being shared in the punishment will not benefit you, and sharing it will not lighten any part of the punishment for you, because each of the disbelievers and the devils has the greatest share of the punishment. Muqatil said: Excuse-making and regret will not benefit you today; you and your companions today share in the punishment just as you shared in the world [in disbelief].

﴿Can you make the deaf hear, or guide the blind, and those who are in manifest error?﴾ That is, the disbelievers upon whom the word of punishment has been decreed, who will not believe.

﴿So whether We take you away﴾ by causing you to die before We punish them, ﴿We will surely take retribution upon them﴾ by killing them after you.

﴿Or We show you﴾ during your lifetime ﴿that which We have promised them﴾ of punishment, ﴿for indeed We are Omnipotent over them﴾, able: whenever We wish, We punish them. By this he meant the polytheists of Makkah, from whom He took vengeance on the Day of Badr; this is the view of most of the commentators. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: By it is meant the people of Islam from the community of Muhammad ﷺ. After the Prophet ﷺ there was severe retribution within his community, but Allah honored His Prophet, took him away, and did not show him in his community anything except what would gladden his eye, and left the retribution after him. It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ was shown what would befall his community after him, and he was never seen laughing or cheerful until Allah took him. [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 25/75, al-Hakim: 2/447, and 'Abd al-Razzaq in his Tafsir: 2/197; al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur: 7/379 also attributed it to 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir.]]

[[A portion of a hadith narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Manaqib, chapter: Virtues of the Quraysh: 6 / 533.]]

Mujahid said: "The people" are the Arabs. The Qur'an is an honour for them in that it was revealed in their language. Then this honour is specially attributed to the most special among the Arabs, and so on, until most of it belongs to the Quraysh and the Banu Hashim.

It was also said: "Its reminder" is an honour for you, by what He has given you of wisdom; "and for your people," the believers, by what Allah has guided them with; "and you will be questioned" about the Qur'an and about what is incumbent upon you of upholding its right.

The Exalted and Majestic said: ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers: Did We appoint gods other than the Most Merciful to be worshipped?﴾ Scholars differed regarding these "questioned":

'Ata' narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: When the Prophet ﷺ was taken on the Night Journey, Allah raised for him Adam and his offspring from among the messengers. Jibril called the adhan and then the iqamah, and said: "O Muhammad, go forward and lead them in prayer." When he finished the prayer, Jibril said to him: "Ask, O Muhammad: 'Those whom We sent before you of Our messengers...'" [the verse]. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I will not ask; I have been sufficed." This is the view of al-Zuhri, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd, who said: Allah gathered the messengers for him on the night of his Night Journey and commanded him to ask them, but he did not doubt and did not ask.

Most of the exegetes said: Ask the believers among the People of the Book to whom Allah sent the prophets: Did not the messengers come to them with nothing but tawhid (the oneness of God)? [[Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: 4 / 130: "That is, all the messengers called to what you have called to... like His saying: (And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, saying: Worship Allah and avoid the false deities)..." **Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 43, verses 72–77:**

﴿And that is the Paradise which you have been given as an inheritance for what you used to do. Therein for you is abundant fruit, from which you will eat.﴾ It is said in a hadith: "No man will pull a fruit from Paradise except that another like it will grow in its place."[[Narrated by al-Tabari: 25/97. Al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (7/392) also attributed it to Abd ibn Humayd. Al-Haythami said in al-Majma' (10/414): "It was narrated by al-Tabarani and al-Bazzar. The narrators of al-Tabarani and one of the two chains of al-Bazzar are trustworthy."]]

﴿Indeed, the criminals﴾, meaning the polytheists, ﴿will abide forever in the punishment of Hell. It will not be lightened for them, and they will be in despair therein. **Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 43, verses 78–83:**

﴿We have indeed brought you the truth﴾. He says: We sent to you, O assembly of Quraysh, Our Messenger with the truth. ﴿But most of you are averse to the truth﴾.

﴿Or have they determined a matter?﴾ That is, have they decided and firmly resolved a matter, in plotting against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? ﴿Then indeed We are determined﴾, that is, We are resolved to requite them. Mujahid said: "If they plot evil, I will plot against them in the same way."

﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private talk?﴾ That is, what they conceal from others and confide to one another in private. ﴿Yes﴾, We hear that and know it. ﴿And Our messengers﴾, that is, the angels, meaning the guardians (al-hafazah), ﴿are with them, recording﴾.

﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾. That is: if the Most Merciful had a son according to your claim and your assumption, then I would be the first to worship him. But He is One, with no partner and no son. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that ﴿if﴾ here means "there is not", so the meaning is: the Most Merciful has no son, and I am the first of the worshippers who bear witness to that. Here "in" (إن) is used with the sense of negation.

Al-Suddi said: its meaning is, "If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first to worship Him on that basis, but He has no son."

It has also been said that "al-'abidin" (الْعَابِدِينَ) means "the disdainful" (الْآنِفِينَ), that is: I am the first of those who reject and deny what you say.

It is also said that the meaning is: I am the first to be incensed that a son should be attributed to the Most Merciful. It is said: "'abada, ya'budu" (عَبَدَ يَعْبُدُ) when one becomes disdainful and angry.

Some people said: it is said "'abada, fahuwa 'abid" (عَبَدَ فَهُوَ عَابِدٌ) is not the usual form; rather one says "fahuwa 'abd" (فَهُوَ عَبْدٌ).

Then He declared Himself free of imperfection, saying: ﴿Glory be to the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, from what they describe﴾, that is, from the lies they utter.

﴿So leave them to plunge into their falsehood﴾ and ﴿to play﴾ in their worldly life, ﴿until they meet their Day which they are promised﴾, that is, the Day of Resurrection.
